original_question: Does every strict conditional independence model for discrete random variables have a Q-rational point? Here a strict conditional independence model is the intersection of the positive orthant with the constructible set of tables for which a specified collection of conditional independence statements Xi ⊥⊥ Xj | XK holds and all other such statements do not hold.
target_in_paper: Section 5, 'Bonus Problem on Rational Points and Brief Conclusion'—specifically the paragraph defining CI varieties, strict CI varieties, strict CI models, and the subsequent 'Bonus Problem'.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the right part of the paper: the bonus problem in Section 5 about discrete conditional independence models and the existence of Q-rational points. It also correctly uses the 'strict' version, namely that certain specified CI statements hold while all other CI statements fail, and it correctly places the model in the positive orthant rather than asking about the entire complex variety.
missing_details: The paper quantifies over all finite families of CI statements among n discrete random variables X1, ..., Xn with prescribed finite state counts d1, ..., dn.
The ambient algebraic object is the CI variety inside the complex tensor space C^{d1} ⊗ C^{d2} ⊗ ··· ⊗ C^{dn}, not just an unspecified set of real tables.
The CI variety is determinantal: it is cut out by the relevant 2×2 minor equations corresponding to the chosen statements Xi ⊥⊥ Xj | X_K.

The strict CI variety is not merely any constructible set; in the paper it is explicitly the subset of the CI variety where no additional CI statement holds, hence a constructible subset that is Zariski open in the CI variety.
The strict CI model is the intersection of that strict CI variety with the positive orthant of real d1×d2×···×dn tables; the paper does not impose a normalization such as total sum 1.

The paper also gives an equivalent description: a strict CI model is one equivalence class of positive tables, where two tables are equivalent exactly when the same CI statements are valid and the same CI statements are not valid for both.
To make 'Q-rational point' stand-alone, one should say explicitly that this means a point of the strict CI model whose table entries are all rational numbers.

The paper's formal open question is the bare existence question above; the further thought about whether rational points might appear once d1, ..., dn are very large is presented only as speculation, not as the main official formulation.
refined_question: Let X1, ..., Xn be discrete random variables with finite state counts d1, ..., dn, and let V ⊂ C^{d1} ⊗ C^{d2} ⊗ ··· ⊗ C^{dn} be the conditional independence variety determined by a chosen collection of statements of the form Xi ⊥⊥ Xj | X_K, i.e. the determinantal variety cut out by the corresponding 2×2 minor equations. Let V^str be the associated strict CI variety, consisting of those tables in V for which exactly the chosen CI statements hold and no other CI statement Xi ⊥⊥ Xj | X_K holds, and let M = V^str ∩ R_{>0}^{d1d2···dn} be the corresponding strict CI model. Must every such strict CI model M contain a point whose coordinates are all rational numbers?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, for every equivalence class of positive d1×d2×···×dn tables under the relation 'two tables are equivalent iff precisely the same conditional independence statements Xi ⊥⊥ Xj | X_K hold for both', does that class contain a table with all entries in Q?
justification: The draft is already close to the paper's intended question, but the nearest paper-faithful target is the Section 5 Bonus Problem, stated for strict CI models, not for arbitrary constructible subsets in the abstract. In that section, the paper first fixes n discrete variables with state counts d1, ..., dn, places the CI variety in the ambient complex tensor space C^{d1} ⊗ ··· ⊗ C^{dn}, recalls that it is determinantal, then defines the strict CI variety by requiring that the chosen CI statements hold and all others fail, and finally defines the strict CI model as its intersection with the positive orthant. The exact open problem is then 'Does every strict CI model have a Q-rational point?' The refined version restores these ambient-space and definitional details, keeps the question narrowly on the model rather than the larger variety, and preserves the paper's no-normalization convention for positive tables.
